kurz: How to determine your needs in retirement from your expenses rather than from your last payslip, and how to derive the pension gap and the capital requirement from them.

bloecke.md:
The question of how much money you need in retirement is almost always approached from the income side. This calculation shows how much pension will result, but says nothing about whether the amount is enough. The reverse order is more informative. First the requirement is determined, then the secured income is established. The difference is the amount that a savings plan has to cover.

Three quantities are enough for this, namely the monthly net requirement in retirement, the monthly net income from all lifelong pensions and the capital that funds the difference over twenty to thirty-five years. Further details merely refine the calculation.

## Expenses that end and new expenses

Your last net salary is a poor yardstick, because it contains items that disappear with your last working day. These include the savings contribution for retirement itself. With a savings rate of 15% of net income, this 15% is by definition no longer needed in retirement. In addition, there are work-related costs such as commuting, a second car, lunches out, work clothing and further training. In many households, the repayments on a property also end by then, and maintenance payments for children run out.

Other expenses rise. These include co-payments and services that the health insurance fund does not cover, such as glasses and dental prosthetics, and later also domestic help and home adaptations. In the first years of retirement, there is often additional spending on travel and on purchases for which there was previously no time. Studies of spending patterns in retirement typically find a U-shape. Spending is high at the beginning and at the end and lower in the years in between. The average is suitable as a planning figure, but it is not sufficient for liquidity planning.

bloecke.formel: Net requirement = last net income − savings contribution − work-related costs − expiring repayment + new expenses
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula replaces the rule of thumb with four items that can be read from your own account statements. The personal replacement rate follows from it as a result and does not have to be assumed.
variablen: disposable household income in the last year of work
everything that regularly goes into retirement provision and wealth building
travel, meals, clothing, membership fees, second home
health, travel, domestic help, higher running costs from spending more time at home
bloecke.beispiel: €2,750 net − €400 savings contribution − €180 work-related costs − €0 repayment + €170 new expenses = €2,340 requirement, that is, 85% of the last net income.

bloecke.md:
## Replacement rate and pension level of 48%

The [[replacement rate]] is the pension divided by previous income. Its value depends entirely on which two figures you use. The statutory [[Pension level (Rentenniveau)|pension level (Rentenniveau)]] of 48.0% is a model ratio. It compares the standard pension from 45 earnings points (Entgeltpunkte) with average earnings, both after social security contributions and before tax. Under current law, a floor (Haltelinie) applies to this value until 2031. The ratio says nothing about any individual person.

The widespread rules of thumb of 70% to 80% of the last net income do not apply generally either. They result mainly from the savings contribution. A household that most recently saved 10% and had hardly any travel costs is more likely to need 90%. With a 25% savings rate and a daily commute of 60 kilometres, 70% is enough. The ratio is therefore a result of the calculation and not an input.

bloecke.titel: The most common misconception about the pension level
bloecke.md: A pension level of 48% does not mean that someone receives 48% of their last salary. The denominator is the average earnings of all insured persons and not your own final salary, and the numerator assumes 45 uninterrupted years on average earnings. For insured persons who most recently earned well above average, the personal ratio is far lower. A career with a steep rise towards the end reinforces this, because the early years with few earnings points remain in the pension account.

## From gross pension to net pension

Social security contributions are deducted from the gross pension first. Pensioners with compulsory insurance pay 7.3% for health insurance plus half of the additional contribution (Zusatzbeitrag) set individually by each health insurance fund. In 2026 this averages 2.9%, so the pensioner's own share is 1.45%. In addition, there is 3.6% for long-term care insurance, or 4.2% for childless persons aged 23 and over. Together this comes to around 12.35%, or around 12.95% for childless persons. The other half of the health insurance contribution is borne by the pension insurance institution, while the pensioner bears the long-term care contribution alone.

The pension is then taxed under Section 22 EStG (Income Tax Act). For pensions starting in 2026, 84% of the annual gross pension is taxable. The remaining 16% is fixed as a set amount in euros in the first full year of the pension. This [[Pension tax-free amount (Rentenfreibetrag)|pension tax-free amount (Rentenfreibetrag)]] stays the same for life, so every later pension increase is fully taxable. Nevertheless, no tax is payable on small pensions. The basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag, in 2026 around €12,348 for single persons), the lump-sum allowance for income-related expenses of €102 (Werbungskostenpauschale) and the deductible health and long-term care insurance contributions are then together at least as high as the taxable portion.

bloecke.titel: Three employment histories, each with 40 contribution years

bloecke.md: The provisional average earnings for 2026 are €51,944. Annual earnings of this amount yield one earnings point. The gross pensions are calculated as earnings points × €42.52. For the net pensions, 12.35% in social security contributions has been deducted. Income tax is estimated roughly, without church tax, without other income and without joint assessment. In case A, the taxable portion stays below the basic tax-free allowance; in case C, around €170 of tax is payable per month.

## Inflation over thirty years

A retirement extends over two to three and a half decades. Over this period, the loss of purchasing power is the largest single item. The ECB aims for an inflation rate of 2% in the euro area over the medium term. At this target, the purchasing power of €1,500 falls to €828 in thirty years. At 3%, it is €618, just under 59% less than at the start.

The statutory pension, by contrast, is not a fixed amount. It is adjusted to wage growth every year on 1 July, in 2026 by 4.24% to €42.52 per earnings point. This protects against inflation, although not completely. In the years 2021 to 2023, the adjustment was below the rate of price increases more than once. A private immediate annuity with a fixed annuity conversion factor does not offer this protection; its payment is fixed in nominal terms. A careful calculation of needs therefore has to include the question of which part of future income is regularly adjusted and which remains fixed in nominal terms.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of the purchasing power of a nominally fixed amount from the start of the pension in 2026 at constant inflation of 2% or 3%.

bloecke.md:
## From the gap to the capital requirement

Once the net requirement and the expected net pension are known, a monthly gap results. A capital stock has to cover this gap over the entire duration of retirement. The methodologically sound approach is to calculate via the present value of an annuity. You calculate in today's purchasing power and apply a **real return**, that is, the return after inflation and after tax. A calculation with nominal returns that ignores inflation considerably overestimates how long the capital will last.

The range of assumptions matters more than the decimal places. For a broadly diversified portfolio of shares and bonds, a real return of 2% in the withdrawal phase is a cautious assumption. A real return of 0% means that the assets are simply used up. The results show immediately how strongly each assumption affects the outcome. A withdrawal period five years longer increases the capital requirement by about as much as one percentage point less return.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula calculates the present value of an annuity paid in arrears over n years at a real return r. At r = 0, the factor simplifies to n. The factor states how many annual amounts of capital are needed.
variablen: real return after inflation and taxes, as a decimal
planned duration of withdrawals in years

bloecke.titel: Capital requirement for a monthly gap of €1,000
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in thousands of euros and today's purchasing power, in which five more years of withdrawals have a similar effect to one percentage point less return.

bloecke.titel: Requirement, gap and capital for the three cases

bloecke.md: During working life, case A and case C are around €41,500 of gross salary a year apart, but only about €81,000 apart in capital requirement. The gross pension grows in proportion to the earnings points. The requirement, by contrast, grows less than proportionally, because households with higher incomes typically had a higher savings rate and more work-related costs. At the upper end, income tax also reduces the increase in the pension. It follows that, relative to income, the capital requirement is hardest to raise for low incomes. In case A it corresponds to just over five annual gross salaries, in case C to just under three and a half. The gap grows considerably more slowly than income, whereas the ability to save grows with it.

As of 1 July 2026, the average co-payment (Eigenanteil) in a care home nationwide is €3,677 a month before the care home supplement (Leistungszuschlag). By federal state, it ranges from €3,190 (Saxony-Anhalt) to €4,105 (Bremen). The supplements under Section 43c SGB XI (Social Code Book XI, long-term care insurance) reduce it with the length of stay to €3,364, €3,051, €2,633 and, after 36 months, €2,111. That is too much to plan for as a monthly item, and a stay in a care home is too rare to assume with certainty. In planning, long-term care costs are therefore treated as a risk at the end of life and covered by a reserve, by owner-occupied property as a last resort or by supplementary insurance. Details are covered in the separate lesson on long-term care and illness.

For recipients of basic income support in old age (Grundsicherung im Alter), only up to €281.50 a month from Riester, Rürup and company pensions as well as lifelong private pensions remains exempt from offsetting in 2026. The first €100 remains fully exempt, plus 30% of the amount above that, in total at most half of standard needs level 1 (Regelbedarfsstufe 1). Everything above that reduces the benefit one for one. Unrestricted portfolio assets, by contrast, are taken into account as assets and not as income, so they are treated in a fundamentally different way. For very small earned incomes, subsidised provision can therefore bring less in arithmetical terms than hoped. The calculation of needs must show this openly.

bloecke.titel: Later start of the pension and additional earnings
bloecke.md:
Two measures have a stronger effect than the savings contribution.

A later start of the pension shortens the withdrawal period and at the same time extends the saving period. If the pension starts at 69 instead of 67, the capital requirement from the table above falls by around 5%. In addition, you save for two years longer, and additional earnings points reduce the gap itself.

The second measure is continuing to work part-time. Since 2023, there has no longer been an additional earnings limit for old-age pensions. Once the standard retirement age has been reached, up to €2,000 a month of employment income is also tax-free under Section 3 no. 21 EStG (Aktivrente). Social security contributions remain payable, and the rule does not apply to the self-employed, to civil servants in respect of their civil service or to mini-jobs. Additional net earnings of €500 a month over five years replace around €28,000 of capital in arithmetical terms.

The target figure is made up of four components: net requirement in today's purchasing power, net pension from all lifelong entitlements, assumed withdrawal period and real return. A percentage of your last salary does not replace this calculation. If one of the components changes, the result changes, and duration, return and requirement have effects of a similar order of magnitude.

The starting point is case B with a gap of €880, 30 years and a real return of 2%, which requires around €237,000 of capital.

- With a withdrawal period of 35 instead of 30 years, the capital rises to around €264,000, that is, by 11%.
- With a real return of 1% instead of 2%, the factor rises from 22.40 to 25.81 and the capital to around €273,000.
- With a requirement 5% lower (€117 a month), the capital falls to around €205,000, that is, by around €31,000.

The last point is often underestimated. A spending base that is permanently 5% lower has about as strong an effect as one percentage point of return, and it is the only one of the three quantities that you decide on yourself.

mitnehmen: The requirement in retirement is derived from the last net income less the savings contribution and work-related costs, and not from a rule of thumb.
The pension level of 48% is a model ratio with average earnings in the denominator and says nothing about your own pension.

Around 12.35% in social security contributions is deducted from the gross pension; for pensions starting in 2026, 84% is taxable under Section 22 EStG, and because the pension tax-free amount is a fixed sum in euros, every increase is taxed in full.
The gap is converted into a capital requirement via the present value of an annuity, using the formula monthly gap × 12 × factor at a real return.
A withdrawal period five years longer changes the result about as much as one percentage point less return, and long-term care is planned as a risk at the end of life and not as a monthly item.

begriffe.text: Ratio of income in retirement to income before retirement. It is only meaningful on a net basis and only if both reference figures are named. The statutory pension level is not a personal replacement rate.

Pre-tax safeguard level (Sicherungsniveau vor Steuern), that is, the ratio of the standard pension from 45 earnings points to average earnings, in each case after social security contributions. In 2026 it is 48.0%; under current law, the floor (Haltelinie) applies until 2031.

The part of the annual pension that remains tax-free at the start of the pension under Section 22 EStG. It is determined as a fixed amount in euros in the first full year of the pension and does not grow with later pension increases.
Number of annual amounts needed as capital to fund a withdrawal over n years at a real return r. The factor is (1 − (1 + r)^−n) / r.

Return after deducting inflation; in retirement planning it is also taken after taxes. If requirement and capital are stated in today's purchasing power, only this return may be used in the calculation.
